title: With RM70,000 at 25, should I start a business or buy property first?
excerpt: A 25-year-old with RM70,000 saved wants to escape the rat race, either with a self-service laundry or rental properties. Sean says start the business first: property keeps you rich rather than making you rich.

question.asker: From C, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: C is 25, lives with his parents, earns a little over RM3,000 a month and has about RM70,000 in savings. He wants to escape the rat race, either by opening a self-service laundry or by building rental properties, and hopes to reach RM5,000 to RM6,000 a month from rent. He fears a failed business would send him back to a job, while buying property would leave no money for the business.
question.text: Should he start the business or the property investment first, and how many rental units would it take to live off rent?

answer.quote: Real estate don't really make you rich, real estate keeps you rich.
answer.summary: Start the business first, carefully and if possible while keeping his job. At 25 with no commitments he can afford to fail, and running a business teaches him far more than a salary does. Once the business makes money, buy properties whose rent covers the instalment, and use them to store that wealth.

reasons.title: Living off rent takes many units and years
reasons.body: A unit with a surplus of RM500 a month after its instalment is already a good one, so RM5,000 to RM6,000 would take about ten such units bought years ago, with the risk that some sit empty.

reasons.title: Positive cash flow comes from time or crafted deals
reasons.body: Sean's Puchong apartment, bought for about RM300,000, only broke even for its first three to five years before rents rose. Otherwise, the deals come from motivated sellers known through specialist agents, or from buying in bulk for a developer discount.

reasons.title: A business teaches what a job can't
reasons.body: Customers, capital and operating costs, hiring, company registration, accounts and the rent versus footfall of a location are all lessons for later wealth. If it fails at 25, he can simply go back to work.

reasons.title: Property compounds quietly
reasons.body: After ten years his tenants had paid his Puchong loan below RM300,000 while the unit was worth about RM400,000, so he could refinance and buy again. Repeating that builds two or three paid-off units by about 60.

actions: Plan the laundry business carefully, with costs, location and footfall, and don't spend all RM70,000 at once.
Keep his job while the business is starting, if he can.
Once the business earns money, buy properties whose current rent covers the instalment.
Expect each unit to give a modest surplus, and let tenants build the equity over time.
Read up on the cash flow quadrant idea of employees, self-employed, business owners and investors.
caveat: Rents rarely jump, so a unit's surplus stays modest unless it is improved. Sean chose a corporate career and property in his early 20s himself, so the right order depends on the path you want.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #193. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in December 2022.
